prime_epop.title: Prime-age employment rate
prime_epop.subtitle: Employed share of the population, ages 25–54
prime_epop.note: Used at two windows in the current videos (data_1995_present.json, data_2019_present.json). Both are slices of this same series; Phase 2's spec windows replace the need for two files.

prime_lfpr.title: Prime-age labor force participation
prime_lfpr.subtitle: Labor force share of the population, ages 25–54
prime_lfpr.note: Companion series to prime_epop -- same BLS LNS convention (12 = employment-population ratio, 11 = labor force participation rate), same age slice, same population base. LFPR >= EPOP always (everyone employed is in the labor force; the gap is the unemployed share). Added for a 2-line 'employment vs. participation' comparison video, not a replacement for prime_epop.

unrate.title: Unemployment rate
unrate.subtitle: Unemployed share of the labor force
unrate.note: Computed from components, not the pre-rounded published UNRATE release, so waypoint ordering stays stable at one decimal on screen even though four decimals are stored. Verified 2026-08-24 against data_unrate_2022_present.json: exact match to 4 decimals for every row in the committed window.

unemployed.title: Unemployed
unemployed.subtitle: Number of unemployed people, seasonally adjusted
unemployed.note: Raw FRED units are thousands of persons. Has a real one-month gap at 2025-10-01 (BLS did not publish that month); buildRuns already renders JSON null as a gap.

openings.title: Job openings
openings.subtitle: Total nonfarm job openings, seasonally adjusted
openings.note: Raw FRED units are thousands. Series starts December 2000 (JOLTS history) — the JSON file itself starts there, no leading nulls, since fetch.R pulls each series alone rather than padding it against a longer one.

vu_ratio.title: Vacancy-to-unemployment ratio
vu_ratio.subtitle: Job openings per unemployed worker
vu_ratio.note: Not used by any current video. Registered now because its title already appears as list-card copy in src/data/cards_full_employment_reasons.json; a chart for it is a plausible near-term ask.

recessions.title: NBER recession indicator
recessions.subtitle: 1 during an NBER-dated recession month, 0 otherwise
recessions.note: Not a chart series -- never plotted or formatted as a value. Phase 4's engine/annotations.ts scans this for contiguous 1-runs to build the built-in "recessions" band shorthand. Fetched through the same registry/fetch.R mechanism as everything else so it gets the same vintage tracking, not because it's a line anyone would draw.

unrate_bls.title: Unemployment rate
unrate_bls.subtitle: Unemployed share of the labor force
unrate_bls.note: Same construction as `unrate` (100 * unemployment level / labor force level) but pulled directly from the BLS public API (LNS13000000 / LNS11000000) instead of FRED's UNEMPLOY/CLF16OV mirror -- for jobs-day use, when BLS publishes before FRED has synced same-day. Requires BLS_KEY in the environment (see data/fetch.R's "bls" source). Kept as a separate registry entry from `unrate` rather than replacing it, per CLAUDE.md Section 11's rule against silently changing a series' source.

payrolls_change_1st.title: Monthly job growth
payrolls_change_1st.subtitle: Nonfarm payrolls, thousands, as first reported
payrolls_change_1st.note: Not a BLS API series -- scraped from the BLS CES revisions table (https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesnaicsrev.htm) by jobs-day/scrape_revisions.py, the same page and parsing logic BLS-CPS-Jobs-Numbers/99_download_jobs_revisions.py uses. `sa_1st` is the FIRST published estimate for each month -- the number that actually printed on that month's jobs day -- not the current (possibly twice-revised) CES0000000001 level, so a given month's value here is frozen once printed. This is deliberately a different number from what a FRED-based `payrolls`-style series would give you by differencing CES0000000001, which reflects only the latest revision. See jobs-day/README.md.

payrolls_change_2nd.title: Monthly job growth (2nd estimate)
payrolls_change_2nd.subtitle: Nonfarm payrolls, thousands, as 2nd reported
payrolls_change_2nd.note: Same scrape/table as `payrolls_change_1st` (see its note) -- `sa_2nd` is that month's SECOND published estimate (one month after the first print), still not the current fully-revised CES0000000001 level. Exists so the jobs-day grouped-bar revisions chart (BarVideo) can show 1st/2nd/3rd side by side, matching BLS-CPS-Jobs-Numbers/01_initial_tweet.R's left panel. See jobs-day/README.md.

payrolls_change_3rd.title: Monthly job growth (3rd estimate)
payrolls_change_3rd.subtitle: Nonfarm payrolls, thousands, as 3rd reported
payrolls_change_3rd.note: Same scrape/table as `payrolls_change_1st` (see its note) -- `sa_3rd` is that month's THIRD published estimate (two months after the first print). BLS considers a print settled after the third estimate, though it can still be touched by later annual benchmark revisions, which this table does not carry. See jobs-day/README.md.

payrolls_change.title: Total employment
payrolls_change.subtitle: Monthly change in total nonfarm payrolls
payrolls_change.note: Deliberately NOT the same number as `payrolls_change_1st`/`_2nd`/`_3rd`. Those are frozen at whichever estimate vintage they name, scraped from BLS's revisions table. This is CES0000000001 (total nonfarm employment level, SA) differenced month-over-month via the BLS API -- so every historical month here reflects however many rounds of revision have landed since, i.e. the CURRENT best-known change, the number a chart drawn today would headline. Matches the `ces = CES0000000001 - lag(CES0000000001, 1)` pattern in BLS-CPS-Jobs-Numbers/00_run_monthly.R and /02_unrate_jobs.R exactly. Pick this one for "what's the picture right now"; pick `payrolls_change_1st` for "what did the headline say that month."
